title: Episode 4 (lines 1115–1200)

teacherSummary.text: The old herdsman of Laius, once a household slave, arrives. The Corinthian identifies him as the man who gave him the baby. The herdsman tries not to answer; Oedipus orders him threatened until he speaks. He admits that the child came from Laius' house and that the queen gave it to him to destroy because of a prophecy; he pitied it and gave it away. Oedipus recognizes the whole truth.

vocabulary.definition: the killing of one's father, or the person who does it
vocabulary.context:
I stand a wretch, in birth, in wedlock cursed,
A parricide, incestuously, triply cursed.
vocabulary.source: Liber et Libri contextual definition, hand-written against the line in Oedipus Rex

etymology.text: “parricide”: Origin: possibly Middle French parricide; earlier Latin parricīda.
etymology.checked: 2026-10-21 (language, form and meaning taken from the Wiktionary entry's etymology templates; wording ours)

context.history: Threatening an enslaved man to make him speak (lines 1160–1167) shows the power masters held over enslaved people; it is wrong, and the play does not hide its cruelty.

significance: Aristotle uses this play as his example of reversal: the messenger who comes to cheer Oedipus produces the opposite effect (Aristotle, ca. 335 B.C.E./1999, ch. XI). The investigator finds himself.
discussionQuestions: Is it ever right to force someone to tell the truth? Why or why not?
Where does plot appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with leadership and the city?

items.prompt: Analyze the significance of Oedipus's cry “O light, may I behold thee nevermore!”
items.expected: Light in the play has stood for knowledge and sight. Now that Oedipus finally sees the truth, he wishes never to look on the light again. The line reverses his earlier promise to make dark things clear: having brought the truth to light, he cannot bear to see it. It turns the theme of sight and blindness against the king.

items.prompt: Evaluate the herdsman's decision to save the infant out of pity. Was it right?
items.expected: His decision was humane: he could not bear to let a baby die. Yet his pity defeated the plan meant to stop the oracle, and the child he saved grew up to fulfil it. The play does not condemn his mercy, but it shows that even kind choices cannot escape fate, which makes his act both good and tragic.

satQuestions.passage:
No wonder, master. But I will revive
His blunted memories. Sure he can recall
What time together both we drove our flocks,
He two, I one, on the Cithaeron range,
For three long summers; I his mate from spring
Till rose Arcturus; then in winter time
I led mine home, he his to Laius’ folds.
Did these things happen as I say, or no?
’Tis long ago, but all thou say’st is true.
Well, thou mast then remember giving me
A child to rear as my own foster-son?
Why dost thou ask this question? What of that?
Friend, he that stands before thee was that child.

The knave methinks will still prevaricate.
Nay, I confessed I gave it long ago.
Whence came it? was it thine, or given to thee?
I had it from another, ’twas not mine.
From whom of these our townsmen, and what house?
Forbear for God’s sake, master, ask no more.
If I must question thee again, thou’rt lost.
Well then—it was a child of Laius’ house.
Slave-born or one of Laius’ own race?
Ah me!
I stand upon the perilous edge of speech.
And I of hearing, but I still must hear.
Know then the child was by repute his own,
But she within, thy consort best could tell.
What! she, she gave it thee?
’Tis so, my king.
With what intent?

anchorPassages.note: Anagnorisis complete: birth, wedlock, and parricide collapse into one cry.
anchorPassages.text:
To make away with it.
What, she its mother?
Fearing a dread weird.
What weird?
’Twas told that he should slay his sire.
What didst thou give it then to this old man?
Through pity, master, for the babe. I thought
He’d take it to the country whence he came;
But he preserved it for the worst of woes.
For if thou art in sooth what this man saith,
God pity thee! thou wast to misery born.
Ah me! ah me! all brought to pass, all true!
O light, may I behold thee nevermore!
I stand a wretch, in birth, in wedlock cursed,
A parricide, incestuously, triply cursed. Exit Oedipus.
